clinical_category: Asthma self-management - individualized trigger identification and avoidance
blueprint_topic: Health-promotion teaching for recognition and reduction of asthma triggers
stem: A nurse helps a client with asthma identify personal triggers that can worsen symptoms. Which group contains recognized asthma triggers?

options.A: Allergens, viral respiratory infections, physical activity, and poor air quality or other inhaled irritants
options.B: Only one universal trigger that is the same for every person with asthma
options.C: Triggers that are relevant only during childhood and no longer affect adults with asthma
options.D: Only prescribed asthma medications, because environmental and infectious exposures do not worsen asthma

rationale: A is correct. Current NHLBI guidance identifies common asthma triggers including indoor and outdoor allergens, infections such as colds and influenza, physical activity, and poor air quality or cold air. Current CDC guidance likewise emphasizes that triggers differ among people with asthma and includes smoke, allergens, infections, chemicals or fragrances, weather, and exercise among recognized triggers. B is incorrect because triggers are individualized. C is incorrect because asthma triggers affect adults as well as children. D contradicts current federal guidance on environmental, infectious, and activity-related triggers.
educational_objective: Teach clients with asthma to identify their own symptom triggers, which may include allergens, respiratory infections, exercise, smoke or other irritants, and poor air quality, and incorporate trigger reduction into an individualized asthma-management plan.
source_organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI/NIH), corroborated by Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Asthma — Causes and Triggers; Managing Asthma; Controlling Asthma
source_version_date: NHLBI asthma pages last updated 2024-04-17 and current at access 2026-08-18; CDC Controlling Asthma page dated 2024-01-22 and current at access 2026-08-18; current 2026 CDC/NIOSH asthma resources also continue to identify allergens, irritants, and physical exertion as triggers
source_locator: NHLBI 'Asthma — Causes and Triggers' → 'Asthma triggers': common triggers include indoor/outdoor allergens, physical activity, infections such as colds/flu/COVID-19, and poor air quality or very cold air. NHLBI 'Managing Asthma' → 'Know your asthma triggers': avoid identified allergens, infection exposures, air pollution, tobacco smoke, and other personal triggers. CDC 'Controlling Asthma' → Key Points: triggers can differ from one person with asthma to another; common triggers include secondhand smoke, dust mites, air pollution, mold, respiratory infections, pollen/allergies, chemicals/fragrances, weather, and physical exercise.
source_claim_supported: Current federal guidance directly supports allergens, respiratory infections, physical activity, poor air quality, smoke, and other irritants as recognized asthma triggers and explicitly supports individualized trigger identification rather than a universal trigger list for every client.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items); this item tests client education for recognition and reduction of modifiable exposures that can worsen a chronic health condition.
correction_summary: Substantive refinement. The original generic NHLBI homepage was replaced with exact current NHLBI and CDC trigger sections. The final item preserves the clinically sound trigger categories, explicitly emphasizes person-to-person variability, and removes padded distractors without adding universal avoidance rules or unsupported exposure thresholds.
audit_findings: The original NHLBI root URL did not provide an exact trigger locator.
Current NHLBI guidance directly lists allergens, infections, physical activity, and poor air quality/cold air among common asthma triggers.
Current CDC guidance explicitly states that asthma triggers differ among individuals and corroborates smoke, allergens, infections, irritants, weather, and exercise as triggers.
The final item avoids implying that all listed triggers affect every client and does not prescribe unsupported universal exposure limits.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no cueing, no unsupported quantitative rule, and no unresolved conflict.
